newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-RUSSIAN SEASON OPENS WITH MATCH-FIXING WARNING.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RUSSIAN SEASON OPENS WITH MATCH-FIXING WARNING.

text.p: Russian clubs kick off their 1997 season on Sunday after a stern warning from the head of the league that match-fixing will be severely punished.
"We must get rid of this dangerous phenomenon," league president Nikolai Tolstykh told a news conference on Friday.

Citing second division Iriston Vladikavkaz, thrown out of the league last year for trying to rig a match, Tolstykh said he understood the financial pressure on clubs for success since the end of Soviet state funding. But the bribery and corruption, long alleged but rarely proven, must be rooted out.
The league has set up a commission to tackle it. Russia's new Criminal Code, which replaced Soviet law this year, gives full legal weight to sanctions against corruption in sport.
Iriston were let back in, to the third and bottom division, this year. But the league says a "get tough" approach will apply to a whole range of major and minor infringements of its rules.

Even the mighty CSKA Moscow, Tolstykh recalled, flirted with exclusion during the close season when an internal split in the Russian army club prompted two rival groups to register for this season. The argument over ownership was quickly settled after the league threatened to simply bar CSKA altogether.

After years of haggling over transfer fees, Tolstykh said, the league "fired a shot across the bows" of clubs who fail to pay for players by docking six points from Olimp Kislovodsk, condemning them to relegation to the third division this year.
The start of the premier league campaign also sees eight of the 18 top flight clubs penalised as part of the league's offensive against sub-standard stadiums and icy pitches.

During the first two rounds of the championship, the eight who failed to install undersoil heating by the start of the season will play their first home fixture at a neutral ground. If the work is not done by September, the teams will lose six points and play their remaining home games away.
"We know it's pretty tough," Tolstykh said.
But the league is determined to get premier league grounds up to FIFA international standards by next season.

As well as cutting the premiership to 16 teams to improve competitiveness, notably in European club tournaments, Tolstykh said he expected up to 40 lower division sides to be kicked out of the league after this season, allowing a big reorganisation.
Champions and firm favourites Spartak Moscow, who have won four of the five post-Soviet pennants, kick off their season on the Black Sea on Sunday against Zhemchuzhina Sochi.

They are not alone. Three other games will be played in Sochi, once the politburo's favourite resort. Three teams which failed to install heating, including last year's third-placed Rotor Volgograd, stage home fixtures there on Sunday and Monday.
Alania Vladikavkaz, runners-up last year and 1995 champions, are at home on Sunday to outsiders KamAZ Naberezhniye Chelny.
Moscow sees one its bitterest derbies of the season, police versus army -- otherwise known as Dynamo against CSKA.

Among the capital's Big Five, CSKA will be under close scrutiny after the mass defection of coach Alexander Tarkhanov and much of his squad to Torpedo Moscow. Ex-Russia trainer Pavel Sadyrin heads CSKA after being sacked by Zenit St. Petersburg.
